items.label: section_header
items.text: 2 ELEMENTS, COMPOUNDS AND MIXTURES

items.label: text
items.text: Most of the substances that we are familiar with from everyday life are mixtures. For example, the air that we breathe is a mixture containing elements such as nitrogen and oxygen, and compounds such as carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxides. The food that we eat and the drinks that we drink are mixtures. This chapter looks at the properties of elements, compounds and mixtures, and also how to separate the components of a mixture. Separation of mixtures is very important in the analysis of substances, such as in forensics.

items.label: section_header
items.text: LEARNING OBJECTIVES

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand how to classify a substance as an element, compound or mixture

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 2.1 Gold is an element, but a gold ring made from 18-carat gold only contains 75% gold. The metal is a mixture of gold and, usually, copper.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 2.2 Pure water is a compound, but the water we drink is a mixture of water and other dissolved substances.

items.label: section_header
items.text: ELEMENTS

items.label: text
items.text: Elements are substances that can't be split into anything simpler by chemical means. An element contains only one type of atom (but see the key point in the margin). In models or diagrams they are shown as atoms of a single colour or size.

items.label: caption
items.text: a pure metal such as magnesium

items.label: caption
items.text: oxygen gas

items.label: caption
items.text: diamond (a form of carbon)

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 2.3 Elements contain only one type of atom.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand how to use the calculation of R, values to identify the components of a mixture

items.label: list_item
items.text: Practical: Investigate paper chromatography using inks/food colourings

items.label: section_header
items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: You might want to look at Chapter 3 if you do not already know the term 'atom'.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: It isn't completely true to say that elements consist of only one type of atom. A better way of saying it would be that all the atoms in an element have the same atomic number. Most elements consist of mixtures of isotopes, which have the same atomic number, but different mass numbers (due to different numbers of neutrons). When we draw diagrams or make models, we aren't usually interested in the differences between the isotopes. Isotopes will be discussed in Chapter 3.
